strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: recovering dynamic 3D muscle deformation from observable skin/pose signals is a genuinely new inverse problem in the vision/graphics literature, and the paper convincingly identifies the gap between surface-only body models and anatomy-aware but inaccessible MRI/FEM approaches.

The SKIM dataset is a substantial and reusable contribution: five subjects with layered skin/muscle/bone meshes, 45 minutes of multi-view RGB with ArUco marker tracking, ground-truth skeletal poses, and residual deformation fields. Releasing data and code supports reproducibility and enables follow-up research.

The technical approach is sound and clearly described: canonical residual estimation via LBS (Eq. 4), decoupled muscle/skin non-linear blendshapes, and biomechanically motivated priors (smoothness, bending, stretching, tangential sliding, and isochoric volume preservation) that resolve the inherent muscle/skin disentanglement ambiguity. The priors are well-formulated with attention to discretization invariance.

Honest and informative evaluation: the paper validates plausibility rather than claiming anatomical ground truth it cannot have, uses thresholded DRE to isolate dynamic regions where LBS fails, and includes meaningful ablations over architecture and each loss term that show all components contribute.

Limitations are candidly discussed (dependence on volumetric template fitting, marker suit requirement, subject-specificity), and the contribution type (Dataset/Benchmark + concept/feasibility model) is judged appropriately: the evidence supports the feasibility claim well.
weaknesses: No ground-truth validation of the internal muscle layer: all supervision and evaluation is via sparse skin markers plus physics-inspired proxies. This is inherent to the problem, but the paper's central claim of recovering 'muscle deformation' is only weakly validated—marker-derived skin residuals indirectly constrain the muscle layer, and the actual muscle geometry could be substantially wrong while still fitting surface data. Quantitative muscle-layer evidence (e.g., comparison against FEM simulation or any anatomical reference) is absent.

Very limited generality: the model is subject-specific and trained/evaluated on only five subjects with no cross-subject generalization experiments reported, which restricts immediate impact and leaves open how much of the benefit comes from per-subject overfitting rather than the method itself.

Baseline coverage is thin: only LBS and HIT are compared. Relevant learned/simulation-based competitors, such as Han et al. [15] (neural muscle-driven skin deformation from FEM data) or layered anatomical models [30, 56], are discussed in related work but not quantitatively evaluated, making the claimed superiority harder to assess.

Some reported numbers invite scrutiny: the deep muscle layer volume deviation remains large (10.35%) and the explanation as a 'realistic physical compromise' is qualitative; HIT's very poor MPME (115 mm) suggests possible evaluation misalignment that deserves more analysis. The DRE columns (> 15, > 20, > 25 mm) report values that are means over highly dynamic regions, but the metric definition is deferred entirely to supplementary material, weakening the main paper's self-containedness.

Writing and presentation issues: duplicated sentences (e.g., end of Sec. 4.2, and the double 'By comparing residuals...' explanation), an undefined marker visibility criterion's effect on training coverage, and key details (marker artifact handling, binding mechanism, metric definitions) relegated to supplementary material. Minor: the 'first method' claim should be softened given Neumann et al. [41] and Han et al. [15] predict muscle-related deformation from visual/synthetic signals.

The suit itself constrains the observable skin (markers occlude surface, fabric alters appearance), so the learned skin residual model may not transfer to unclad bodies—an interaction between data acquisition and the learned model that is not analyzed.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: recovering volumetric muscle deformation from accessible multi-view RGB rather than MRI/CT or physics simulation, with a clear gap analysis in the related-work section.

The SKIM dataset contribution is valuable: a multi-layer capture (skin, muscle, bone meshes, marker bindings, ground-truth poses, deformation fields) over 45 minutes per subject for five subjects, with data and code reportedly released, enabling future work on a problem that previously lacked real-world dynamic data.

The technical design is sensible: decoupled muscle/skin residual blendshapes supervised on canonical residuals (pose-invariant loss), plus biomechanically motivated regularizers (biharmonic smoothing, stretch, tangential sliding, volume preservation) to resolve the inherent disentanglement ambiguity.

Evaluation includes ablations across architecture and loss components, and reports physics-plausibility metrics (intersection ratio, volume preservation) in addition to tracking accuracy, with honest discussion of remaining deep-layer volume error (10.35%).
Limitations are candidly stated (initialization dependence, marker-suit requirement, subject-specific models), which is appropriate for the claims made.
weaknesses: The core claim—accurate recovery of internal muscle deformation—is never validated against any volumetric ground truth. All quantitative evidence is skin-level marker tracking plus self-consistency physics metrics computed by the authors' own regularizers. The internal muscle predictions could be substantially wrong in ways these metrics cannot detect, yet the abstract claims 'anatomically grounded' results and 'accurately animates both layers'.

The method is person-specific, and the dataset contains only five subjects. There is no cross-subject generalization experiment, so the claim of a scalable, cost-effective alternative to simulation is only weakly supported; scalability currently means 'feasible in a 120-camera studio with a custom suit'.

The baseline comparison is thin and potentially unfair. HIT [24] is a static, generic-template method applied cross-topology via ad-hoc barycentric marker mapping, which plausibly explains its catastrophic tracking errors (115mm MPME). No comparison against muscle-simulation-based or learned-skin-deformation baselines (e.g., Neumann et al. [41] for arm bulges, Han et al. [15]) is provided.

The 'first method to recover muscle deformations from multi-view RGB' claim overstates novelty: Neumann et al. [41] captured and modeled arm-muscle deformations from RGB, and several cited works predict muscle shape from pose with simulated supervision [15]. The novelty is mainly in scope (full-body, real data), which should be stated more carefully.

Writing and referencing quality is below venue standard: a duplicated sentence explaining canonical-residual pose invariance (Sec. 4.2), duplicated references ([4]/[5]; duplicate DOIs in [21]), a placeholder-looking reference [8] dated 2026 with no venue, product URLs as references, and an inconsistently formatted entry [44]. Table 1's caption ('✓ indicates methods that use real-world data but are limited to static poses...') contradicts the check-mark semantics for the 'Ours' row and is confusing.

Some methodological details that affect reproducibility and correctness are deferred entirely to supplementary material (marker seam handling, temporal filtering, muscle binding, metric definitions, baseline configurations), leaving the main paper's experimental setup under-specified.

The claimed benefit over LBS in the DRE metric (>25mm regions) is presented as evidence of muscle-bulging capture, but DRE is defined against the authors' own tracked markers; high-frequency dynamics improvements may partly reflect tracking smoothing rather than learned anatomy. A perceptual or anatomist evaluation would strengthen the qualitative claims, which currently rest on a few figures.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: to the best of my knowledge this is indeed the first attempt to recover explicit, spatio-temporal 3D muscle deformations from multi-view RGB observations, filling a clear gap between surface-only body models and MRI/FEM-based internal anatomy approaches.

Substantial resource contribution: the SKIM dataset (5 subjects, 45 minutes of multi-view RGB, dense marker tracking, individualized skin/muscle/bone meshes, ground-truth poses, and residual deformation fields) with an announced release of data and code provides a valuable foundation for follow-up work.

Technically sound pipeline: the canonical marker-to-muscle binding via ray casting, inverse-LBS residual estimation in canonical space (pose-invariant supervision), and the decoupled muscle/skin blendshape formulation are clearly derived and well-specified, with most implementation details delegated appropriately to the supplementary material.

Bio-mechanically motivated regularization is thoughtfully designed (area-normalized Laplacian/biharmonic terms, tangential sliding constraints, prism-based signed volume preservation evaluated in appropriate canonical/posed spaces), and the disentanglement ambiguity between muscle and skin layers is honestly identified and addressed.

Reasonably thorough evaluation for this problem setting: comparisons against kinematic (LBS) and volumetric (HIT) baselines across tracking, dynamic-region, intersection, and volume metrics, plus informative ablations over architecture, vector regularizers, and physical energies that justify each design choice.

Candid limitations section acknowledging template-initialization sensitivity, the marker-suit requirement, and the subject-specific nature of the model. Societal-relevant privacy arguments for avoiding medical imaging are made without overclaiming.
weaknesses: Fundamental validation gap: since no in-vivo volumetric ground truth exists during motion, muscle deformation quality is never directly measured. All quantitative evidence comes from skin-surface markers; the claim of 'anatomically grounded' muscle recovery rests on the rest-pose volumetric fitting [30] plus physics priors, which is plausible but unverified. Per-muscle predictions (Fig. 7) are shown qualitatively only, with no metric of muscle shape accuracy.

The markers are on a stretchable fabric suit, not the skin itself. Fabric-skin relative motion, suit tension, and damping could attenuate or distort the soft-tissue signal the method is trained on; the paper asserts tight contact but does not quantify this error source.

Quantitative gains are mixed: SOMA is worse than LBS on MPME (13.43 vs 13.11 mm) and the deep muscle layer (M→B) retains a 10.35% volume deviation, which the authors rationalize as a physical compromise but which weakens the volumetric fidelity claim for the primary muscle layer.

The HIT baseline is evaluated via SMPL topology with markers mapped by barycentric interpolation, which may disadvantage a generic-template method relative to a person-specific one; the striking HIT failure (115 mm MPME, 7.61% intersection) could partly reflect cross-topology artifacts rather than method inferiority. No comparison to person-specific soft-tissue alternatives (e.g., Neumann et al. [41] adapted, or a plain single-layer corrective blendshape without the muscle layer) is provided to isolate the benefit of the muscle layer itself.

Small scale and limited generalization evidence: 5 subjects, studio-only capture, person-specific training, and evaluation on unseen poses only within the same subjects. Claims of 'scalable and cost-effective' solutions are not yet demonstrated; no cross-subject or leave-one-subject-out experiment is reported.

Presentation issues: a duplicated near-identical sentence on p. 9 ('By computing this loss... / By comparing residuals...'), a suspicious incomplete reference [8] ('Botsch, M.: Skeletal-driven animation... (2026)') that reads like a self-citation to unpublished work, and duplicate entries for references [4]/[5] and [21] DOIs reduce polish.

Many critical details (ArUco seam handling, temporal filtering, HIT baseline configuration, metric definitions, the individual-muscle binding mechanism) are deferred entirely to the supplementary material, so the main paper alone does not permit full assessment of reproducibility of the pipeline.

strengths: Novel problem framing: to the authors' knowledge this is the first attempt to recover explicit, subject-specific 3D muscle deformations from visual (RGB-derived) surface observations, addressing a genuine gap between surface-only body models and simulation/medical-imaging-based anatomical models.

Substantial and well-motivated data contribution: the SKIM dataset (5 subjects, ~225 minutes of multi-view capture, 2310 ArUco markers, individualized skin/muscle/bone templates, ground-truth poses, residuals, and visibility masks) is documented in detail in the supplementary material, and data and code are stated to be released, supporting reproducibility.

Technically coherent model: the decoupled muscle/skin blendshape formulation with canonical-space residual supervision (Eq. 4, 7-8) is pose-invariant and clearly derived; the biomechanically-inspired regularization (Laplacian, biharmonic, stretching, tangential sliding, prism-volume preservation with exact signed volumes) is well motivated and mathematically specified (including the supplementary prism-volume derivation).

Reasonable evaluation design: comparison against an LBS kinematic lower bound and a volumetric predictor (HIT), plus thorough ablations (architecture, vector regularization, physical energies) that show each prior's effect on tracking, intersection, and volume metrics; limitations are honestly discussed (subject-specificity, marker suit requirement, unmodeled co-contraction, remaining 10.35% deep-tissue volume deviation).
Clear writing and good figures that communicate the pipeline, dataset structure, and qualitative muscle-activation behavior.
weaknesses: Circularity in the 'ground truth': the internal muscle geometry is derived from a heuristic volumetric fitting [33] of the static scan, and marker-to-muscle correspondences are obtained by ray casting onto this template. Supervision of the muscle layer is therefore heuristic-derived, not measured in vivo, so the claim of learning 'real-world' muscle dynamics is weaker than stated; the muscle layer is effectively supervised only indirectly through skin-marker residuals plus priors, raising questions about whether predicted internal deformations reflect true anatomy.

The claim of 'recovering muscle deformation from multi-view RGB data' is somewhat overstated: RGB is used only for dataset acquisition; at inference the model consumes ground-truth skeletal poses θ from a 120-camera mocap system, not RGB. No experiment demonstrates robustness to estimated (noisy) poses from RGB video.

Limited external validity: evaluation is subject-specific with no cross-subject generalization test despite 5 subjects; internal plausibility is measured only with physics-inspired proxies (intersection ratio, volume change), and no validation against any independent anatomical reference (e.g., MRI) is attempted.

Baseline comparison fairness is questionable: HIT is run via SMPL with a generic template and cross-topology barycentric mapping, which the authors themselves acknowledge causes misalignment; a stronger like-for-like baseline (e.g., a single-layer or MLP variant trained on the same data, partially covered in ablations) would better isolate the contribution of the multi-layer coupled formulation.

The disentanglement between muscle and skin layers is acknowledged as ambiguous and is resolved by hand-tuned asymmetric regularization weights (λ^M vs λ^S); no sensitivity analysis of these weights or of the arbitrary λ choices (e.g., λ_vol = 1000) is provided.

Presentation issues that should be fixed: duplicated sentence in Sec. 4.2, duplicate references ([4]/[5]), an implausible '2026' reference ([9]), and minor supplementary artifacts ('SM/' in Fig. 5, Eq. 11 formatting).

The remaining 10.35% deep-tissue (M→B) volume deviation is justified as a 'physical compromise' but suggests the volume constraints do not fully capture muscular inflation, and the practical impact of this compromise on downstream biomechanical use cases is not analyzed.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely novel and under-explored inverse problem — recovering volumetric muscle deformation from surface/pose observations — and the positioning against surface-only body models, MRI-based inverse anatomy, and FEM/biomechanical simulation is well argued (Table 1 summary is helpful).

The SKIM dataset is a substantial engineering effort: 5 subjects, custom ArUco-embedded suit, 120-camera capture, ~225 minutes of recordings, multi-layer canonical anatomy, and released data/code, which could seed follow-up research even if the modeling contribution is incremental.

The decoupled muscle/skin blendshape formulation with bio-mechanically inspired priors (Laplacian, biharmonic, stretch, tangential sliding, prism-volume preservation via Gauss-Legendre quadrature) is carefully derived, and the Supplementary Material documents parameters, refinement, and the prism-volume derivation with reasonable transparency.

Ablations (architecture, vector regularization, physical energies) are informative and support the design choices; the DRE metric isolating highly dynamic regions and honest reporting of the residual 10.35% deep-tissue volume error show awareness of limitations.
Limitations are candidly discussed (template initialization errors, marker suit requirement, no co-contraction modeling, subject-specific models).
weaknesses: The central scientific claim is weakly validated: there is no ground truth for internal muscle deformation. The 'ground truth' internal layer is itself produced by a heuristic volumetric fitting (Komaritzan et al. [33]) plus ray-cast marker-to-muscle association from the same surface observations the model consumes, and individual muscles are animated purely by barycentric propagation from the boundary layer. The network can therefore succeed by re-encoding the skin signal rather than recovering true muscle dynamics, and the evaluation cannot falsify this.

The marker-suit protocol introduces a serious confound that is never addressed: markers are attached to a fabric suit, so the primary training signal measures suit-skin slippage and suit dynamics rather than actual skin deformation, let alone muscle bulging. No calibration or quantification of suit-skin relative motion is provided.

Quantitative comparisons are against weak or poorly adapted baselines: LBS is a deliberately crippled lower bound, and HIT is evaluated cross-topology via SMPL shape fitting, which conflates HIT's limitations with generic-template and SMPL-fitting errors (its 115mm MPME suggests an unfair setup rather than a meaningful comparison). No baseline from the closely related muscle-deformation learning literature (e.g., Han et al. [17]) is included.

Key evaluation metrics are partially circular: Volume Preservation is computed against the method's own rest-state prism geometry, and Intersection/Volume metrics on layers that were constructed by the same pipeline do not establish anatomical correctness.

Scalability and cost-effectiveness claims in the abstract are undermined by the requirements: a 120-camera studio, 140-camera scanner, custom-manufactured per-subject suit, manual UV-annotation of markers, and person-specific training. Only 5 subjects are captured, evaluation is on unseen poses within subjects (not unseen subjects), so no cross-subject generalization is demonstrated.

Temporal behavior is neither modeled nor evaluated despite the 'spatio-temporal' framing — there is no temporal loss, no jitter/flicker metric, and capture is only 25 Hz; dynamic claims rest on per-frame regression.

Presentation and rigor issues: duplicated sentence in Sec. 4.2; references [4]/[5] are duplicates; reference [9] is a future-dated 2026 citation ('Botsch, M., 2026') that cannot be verified; the internal layer is denoted 'muscle' though it is a fitted volumetric approximation, which risks overstating anatomical fidelity; Table 1's checkmark semantics conflate 'real-world data' with static/heuristic use, arguably overclaiming novelty relative to Neumann et al. [44].

The DRE thresholds (15/20/25mm) are defined relative to baseline LBS error, so the metric is defined post-hoc on regions where the chosen baseline fails; a more standard held-out surface reconstruction error would be more convincing.

strengths: Novel problem formulation: to the authors' knowledge, this is the first attempt to recover full-body, subject-specific 3D muscle deformation from multi-view RGB observations, filling a genuine gap between surface-only body models and inaccessible MRI/CT-based anatomical methods (Table 1 positioning is convincing).

SKIM is a substantial new dataset contribution: 5 subjects with varied demographics, ~45 minutes each at 25 Hz, ~33.7M 2D detections / 266K 3D frames, with multi-layer anatomy (skin, global muscle, bone, 320K-vertex individual muscles), marker trajectories, residuals, and visibility masks. The detailed capture protocol, marker encoding (multi-instance ArUco), annotation tool, and refinement pipeline (supplementary Secs. 1-2, 5) are described with commendable reproducibility detail, and data/code are stated to be released.

Technically sound formulation: decoupled muscle/skin blendshapes with a residual offset, pose-invariant canonical residual supervision (Eqs. 5-8), and a well-motivated set of biomechanical priors (smoothness, biharmonic, stretch, tangential sliding, signed-prism volume preservation with an exact Gauss-Legendre quadrature derivation). The ablations (Tabs. 3-4) show each component contributes, and the honest discussion of the 10.35% deep-layer volume error as a physical compromise adds credibility.

Results are plausible: large improvements in tail errors (P90 19.20 vs 26.03 for LBS; DRE > 25 mm 64.52 vs 134.28) and intersection ratio (0.85% vs 7.61% for HIT), plus qualitative per-muscle visualizations and a real-time interactive tool.
The limitations section is candid and meaningful (template initialization dependency, marker suit requirement, unmodeled co-contraction/force variation, subject-specificity).
weaknesses: The central claim - recovering accurate muscle deformation - is only indirectly validated. No ground truth exists for internal muscle geometry, the muscle layer M is never directly supervised by data (markers supervise only the skin), and no experiment probes muscle-layer accuracy against any independent source (e.g., static MRI/CT of a subject at rest, or FEM simulation). Claims about muscle bulge correctness rest on qualitative figures and physics-inspired proxies.

Evaluation design has circularity and confounds: DRE is defined via markers where 'baseline LBS error exceeds τ', embedding the baseline into the metric; the HIT comparison is confounded by cross-topology transfer (SMPL fitting, barycentric marker mapping), and HIT's high MPME (115 mm) suggests a pipeline failure rather than a fair comparison. There is no strong dynamic baseline (e.g., a learned soft-tissue model such as SoftSMPL adapted to this setting).

On the primary global metric, the method is not better than the trivial baseline (Ours MPME 13.43 vs LBS 13.11); gains are confined to MedPME/P90/DRE. The deep-tissue volume error (10.35%) remains large, so 'anatomical plausibility' is only partially achieved.

Temporal modeling is absent despite claims of 'spatio-temporal muscle behavior': the model maps a single pose θ to displacements with no dynamics (velocity, hysteresis, muscle pumping), even though the dataset's Part III explicitly captures pumping effects that the model cannot represent.

Scale and generalization are limited: 5 subjects, per-subject models, no cross-subject or cross-pose-registry generalization experiments, and the suit may itself alter/filter true skin deformation (fabric sliding, tension), which is not analyzed.

Presentation and scholarship issues that should be fixed: duplicated sentence in Sec. 4.2 (pages 9, 'By computing this loss...' repeated), duplicate references [4]/[5], a citation to a '2026' reference [9] with no venue, oddly formatted reference [47] ('[SIGGRAPH 2025] MAGNET'), and a Table 1 in which 'Ours ✓✓✓' plus the caption's redefinition of '✓' is confusing.
No user study or perceptual evaluation, and no error analysis of how marker-suit coverage (65-95% per motion) biases training/evaluation toward visible regions.
